title: One goal gets the front seat
description: Several goals can ride along, but only one can drive; choosing a single priority for a season makes the rest easier too.

body.heading: Everything cannot be the priority
paragraphs: Most of us carry a kind crowd of goals: get fitter, save more, learn the language, finish the project, be more present. Each is worthy. The trouble is arithmetic — a week only holds so many hours, and goals that all shout at once tend to get a little of us each and enough of us none.
Choosing one front-seat goal for a season is not abandoning the others. It is giving one of them enough of you to actually move, while the rest ride along at maintenance level.

body.heading: How to choose this season’s driver
paragraphs: Ask which goal would make the others easier if it moved — energy, money, calm and confidence tend to unlock a lot. Or ask which one your future self would most thank you for. Either question usually surfaces a clear answer.

Then define what front-seat treatment means in practice: it gets the best time slot, the first claim on spare energy, and protection when the week gets busy. The other goals get a deliberately small keeping-warm version, written down so they do not have to nag.

body.heading: Rotate without guilt
paragraphs: A season is a few months, not forever. When the front-seat goal reaches a natural milestone — or when life changes — hold a small rotation: thank the old driver, choose the next. The back-seat goals were never dropped; their turn simply comes in order.
People often find the rotation itself restful. Instead of five goals murmuring all the time, there is one clear voice and a queue that everyone trusts.

takeaway: Let one goal drive each season, keep the others warm, and rotate on purpose.
